transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, my regular doctor is the one who actually sent me here. It’s honestly just... it's a lot of fuss over nothing, if you want my true opinion on it. Everyone is making this huge, massive deal because they say my weight has dropped too low. My doctor, my family, they’re all just hovering and making a fuss, constantly checking in and worrying. 

But I keep trying to explain to them—and nobody really seems to listen to this part—but I'm a carpenter. I have my shop to run, and I'm on my feet all day long, moving around, lifting things, getting under tables and machinery. I honestly feel like being this light helps me keep up with the shop. I have to be quick, you know? I can't afford to get slowed down. If I were heavier, I’d just be dragging my feet by two o'clock in the afternoon, but staying light keeps me efficient and moving fast. But, well, they just look at the number on the scale and suddenly everyone panics and now I'm sitting here talking to you about it.
Can you tell me approximately what you weigh now, and has your weight changed significantly over the past few months?

Well, I don't really keep track of the exact numbers, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. I know my regular doctor's nurse wrote something down on her little clipboard last week when I was there, but I didn't look and I certainly didn't ask. I just... I don't see the point in obsessing over what some piece of metal on the floor says, you know? 

As for whether it's changed significantly over the past few months... I mean, maybe a little? I haven't really noticed a huge difference myself, but you have to understand, the past few months have been incredibly, incredibly busy for me at the shop. I took on this massive custom cabinetry order for a client out in the valley—beautiful cherry wood, just gorgeous, but heavy, so heavy—and I was working twelve, sometimes fourteen-hour days just cutting and sanding and assembling. When you're in the zone like that, with sawdust everywhere and the noise of the router going, you just don't stop to think about, you know, stepping on a scale or measuring yourself. 

So sure, maybe my toolbelt has been sitting a little looser on my hips lately. I've had to pull my leather belt in a notch or two so my work jeans don't sag when I'm bending over the sawhorses, but I really couldn't give you an actual number. It's just natural fluctuation when you're working hard with your hands all day, don't you think? My sister came by the shop the other day and practically gasped, acting like I was just vanishing into thin air, but I told her, I'm just burning off whatever I don't need to get the job done. It's just efficiency. So no, I don't have a specific weight for you, it's just... whatever it needs to be for me to keep working.
Would you say that others have expressed concern that you look too thin or underweight, even if you feel your weight is appropriate for your work?

Well, yes, I suppose they have. It’s actually become quite the topic of conversation around the shop, which is honestly just exhausting. My husband, for one, he’s always been a bit of a worrier, bless him, but lately he’s just relentless. He’ll come out to the shop with a plate of something or other and just stand there, watching me work, and he’ll say things like, "You’re fading away, you look too thin," and all this dramatic nonsense. And it’s not just him. The apprentices—I have two young guys working with me right now, good kids, but they don’t know a thing about hard work—they’ve started chiming in too. They’ll look at me sideways when I’m lifting a sheet of plywood and ask if I need help, looking at me like I’m about to snap in half. 

I keep telling them, over and over, that I’m perfectly fine. I try to explain it to them, I really do. I tell them that what they’re seeing isn’t sickness, it’s just discipline. It’s what happens when you’re dedicated to your craft and you don’t spend half your day sitting around eating donuts in the breakroom like they do. I mean, you have to be disciplined in this line of work. If you let yourself go, you lose your edge, your precision. But they just don’t get it. They look at me and they see someone who’s "too thin," but I look at myself and I see someone who is stripped down to exactly what’s necessary to get the job done right. It’s incredibly frustrating that people are constantly confusing my discipline and my work ethic with some kind of illness. It’s like they can’t comprehend that someone might actually want to be lean and efficient.
When people say you look too thin, do you see yourself the same way, or do you feel like they’re misunderstanding what they’re seeing?

Well, like I was just saying about my husband and those boys at the shop, they keep saying I look too thin, but they are absolutely, completely misunderstanding what they're looking at. It is a massive misunderstanding. When I look in the mirror—not that I spend hours staring at myself, I don't have that kind of time with the business to run and clients calling constantly—but when I do look, I don't see this frail, vanishing person they keep going on and on about. I see someone who is streamlined. 

I tell them, I tell them all the time that I am perfectly fine. But it's like talking to a brick wall, honestly. People these days, they see someone who doesn't overindulge, someone who runs a tight ship with their own body, and they immediately think there's a problem. They are entirely confusing discipline with sickness. It's exactly that. It's like, if you aren't soft, if you aren't carrying around all this extra padding, suddenly you must be ill. But you don't get to be a fifty-nine-year-old woman running a full-scale custom carpentry shop by being weak or sick. You do it through sheer discipline. 

And my husband, bless his heart, he should know better, he really should. We've been married a long time, he knows exactly how I operate. But he just gets this idea in his head, and the apprentices, well, they're young, they just parrot whatever they hear or whatever they see on the internet. I tell them all, I am fine. I'm more than fine, I'm at peak efficiency. I can fit into tighter spaces to install baseboards, I can move around the shop without knocking into the joinery equipment, I don't get winded just walking across the floor. They look at my arms and see a lack of fat, but I see the muscle and sinew that actually gets the heavy sanding done. So no, I do not see myself the way they do. Not at all. I just see someone who has stripped away the excess, and it honestly baffles me, it really does, that they can't see the difference between being sick and just being incredibly dedicated to your work.
When you look in the mirror, do you ever feel like you still look overweight, even when others say you're too thin?

Well, no, I wouldn't say I look in the mirror and think I'm overweight, not in the traditional sense, anyway. I mean, I don't look at myself and think, "Oh, I'm fat," because that just wouldn't be accurate, would it? But it's more complicated than that, it really is. It's not about being overweight, it's about... it's about the details, the specific areas that just aren't quite right yet. 

Like I was saying before about being streamlined and efficient—when I look in the mirror, I'm looking for the parts that are still getting in the way. I'll look at my upper arms, for instance. Now, I use my arms all day, every day. Lifting, sanding, sawing. They need to be pure muscle, just absolute power and efficiency. But sometimes I look in the mirror, especially under those harsh fluorescent lights we have in the shop bathroom—terrible lighting, really, it casts shadows everywhere—and I'll see this... this softness. Just a little bit of softness right around the triceps, or maybe around my waist where my toolbelt sits. And I think, "That's not necessary. That's excess." 

It's not that I think I'm obese, it's that I see these pockets of inefficiency that I haven't managed to strip away yet. And it's so frustrating, because I work so hard, I put in so many hours, and yet there's still this... this slack. So while my husband and the apprentices are gasping and acting like I'm wasting away, I'm standing there looking at the mirror thinking, "You have no idea what you're talking about, look at this softness here, look at how this isn't perfectly tight." 

It's about the standard I hold myself to, you see. In custom cabinetry, if a joint is off by a millimeter, the whole piece is ruined. It's ruined. You have to be exact. And I just apply that same exactness to myself. So no, I don't see an overweight person, but I definitely, absolutely see someone who isn't finished yet, someone who still has work to do to get to that point of perfect, absolute efficiency. I just don't understand why everyone else can't see the work that still needs to be done.
Do you ever engage in specific behaviors—like restricting your food intake, exercising more, or other routines—to maintain or further reduce your current weight or body shape?

Well, "restricting" is such a... a clinical word, isn't it? It makes it sound like some sort of punishment, which it absolutely isn't. I prefer to think of it as just being practical about my time and my energy, keeping things as efficient as possible. 

Take my workshop days, for instance. When I'm in the shop, I am entirely in the zone. I've got the saws running, the measurements have to be exact down to the fraction of an inch, I've got wood glue setting up, clamps that need to be adjusted... you can't just drop everything because the clock happens to strike noon. It doesn't work like that. So, on workshop days I usually just have tea. I'll make a large thermos of black tea in the morning to keep me going, and maybe, just maybe, I'll have a few careful bites of something small if I really feel like I need to. But honestly, most of the time I don't. 

Because stopping for a real meal... it just feels completely unnecessary. It really does. If I were to stop and sit down and eat a whole sandwich or a plate of whatever heavy thing my husband tries to push on me, it completely throws off the control I’ve got over the day. It breaks my concentration. You eat a big meal and suddenly all your blood is rushing to your stomach, you feel heavy, you feel sluggish, and you lose that... that sharpness. 

I see it with the apprentices all the time. They'll order these massive, greasy meatball subs or pizzas for lunch, and they sit around laughing and eating, and then by two o'clock they are practically asleep on their feet. They're dragging, they're making mistakes, they aren't paying attention to the grain of the wood. I simply cannot afford to be like that. I have a business to run. I have to maintain that tight control from the moment I walk in the door to the moment I lock up at night. 

So my routine is just... keeping things minimal. Keeping the engine running on exactly what it needs and not a single drop more. It's about maintaining that momentum, that absolute, unbroken focus. If you stop to eat a big meal, you lose the rhythm of the project. So yes, I suppose you could say I keep my intake very, very precise. I just don't see it as a problem. It's just how I have to operate to keep everything tight and under my control.
Do you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or push yourself to exercise beyond what is needed for your work, in order to manage your weight or shape?

Vomit? Heavens, no. No, no, no. That is... well, frankly, that just sounds incredibly messy and completely counterproductive. I mean, think about it from a purely practical standpoint. If I were doing something like that, or taking... what did you say, laxatives? If I were taking pills to deliberately upset my system, I wouldn't be able to trust my own body, would I? And in my line of work, you have to trust your body implicitly. 

Imagine being in the middle of routing a delicate edge on a piece of cherry wood—and cherry is beautiful, it really is, but it burns so easily if you hesitate even for a second, you have to keep the router moving at exactly the right speed with exactly the right pressure—and suddenly having to drop everything and run off to the bathroom because of some pill? It’s absurd. It’s a complete loss of control, and as I’ve been telling you, I am all about maintaining absolute control and efficiency. So no, none of that nonsense. It just doesn't fit into my day. My body is a tool, just like my chisels or my block planes, and you don't deliberately damage or destabilize your tools if you want them to perform. 

And as for exercise... well, why on earth would I need to push myself to do more outside of the shop? People who go to gyms and run on treadmills like hamsters on a wheel, they do that because they sit at desks all day. They stare at screens and their bodies go soft. I am on my feet for ten, twelve hours a day. I am hauling sheets of three-quarter-inch MDF, which, let me tell you, is incredibly heavy and awkward for one person to carry, though I manage it just fine because I have the right technique and I don't have any dead weight on my frame holding me back. I'm hoisting upper cabinets into place, I'm squatting down to check baseboard alignments, I'm sanding, I'm sawing, I'm constantly in motion. 

By the time I lock up the shop at night, I have expended exactly the amount of physical energy required to do my job perfectly. Adding some sort of... I don't know, jogging routine or aerobics class on top of that? It would be entirely redundant. A complete waste of time and energy. And I absolutely despise wasting time. If I have any extra time, I'm using it to draw up new schematics or balance the books, not jumping around in a gymnasium. So no, I just stick to the work. The work provides all the physical output I need to keep everything perfectly tight and functioning exactly the way I need it to.
Would you say that how you see yourself—your body shape or weight—has a strong impact on how you feel about yourself overall?

Impact on how I feel about myself? No... no, I really don't think so. I mean, my body is just... it's just the vehicle, isn't it? It's a tool. I don't base my self-worth on what a tape measure says around my waist. I base it on what the tape measure says when I'm checking the diagonal on a set of custom built-ins to make sure they're perfectly square. That's what actually matters. 

If you want to know what impacts how I feel about myself, you should come down to the shop and look at the dovetail joints on the drawers I finished yesterday. We're doing a full kitchen remodel for this couple over in the Heights—beautiful old Victorian home, but of course, nothing is plumb, the floors are sagging, the walls are bowed. It is an absolute nightmare to fit rigid cabinetry into a space like that, frankly. But I spent three days—three full days—making sure the scribe on the baseboards perfectly matched the roll of their original hardwood floors. And when I slid that final piece in, and there wasn't a gap wider than a piece of paper... that is what makes me feel good about myself. That precision. That absolute dedication to getting it right when most contractors would just slap some caulk on it and call it a day. 

My body shape? It's just a byproduct of that same dedication. It's like... well, it's like keeping my chisels sharp. I don't sit around admiring my chisels, patting myself on the back just for having a sharp blade. That would be ridiculous. I just keep them sharp so they cut the wood cleanly without tearing out the grain. It's exactly the same with my body. I keep it stripped down and efficient so I can haul that lumber, so I can fit into tight spaces under a counter to adjust a toe-kick, so I can work a fourteen-hour day without my back giving out or getting winded. 

So, no, I don't look in the mirror and think, "Oh, I'm a good person because I have a certain body shape." That's so superficial. That's what people who have nothing real to show for their lives do, the people obsessed with magazines and vanity. I judge myself by the work. By the fact that my cabinets will still be standing, perfectly level and solid, fifty years after I'm gone. If I make a mistake on a cut, if I let a piece of work go out the door that isn't absolutely flawless... that will keep me up at night. That will ruin my entire week, it makes me sick to my stomach just thinking about doing a sloppy job. But my weight? No. I'm just keeping the machine tuned so it can do the work. I really don't see why my husband or anyone else gets so hung up on the physical aspect of it when the work is what actually speaks for you in the end.
Do you ever feel intense fear or anxiety about gaining weight or becoming heavier, even if you know it might be necessary for your health?

Fear? I wouldn't call it fear. That implies I'm sitting around trembling at the thought of a number on a scale, which I'm not. But... anxiety? A sense of unease? Yes, absolutely. I suppose you could say that. But it's not about the weight itself, not exactly. It's about what the weight represents. It represents a loss of control. It represents letting go of the standards I've set for myself. 

You see, if I let myself slip—if I were to sit down and eat something heavy, something rich, like... well, like the things my husband used to make for the holidays. He used to make this incredible standing rib roast for Christmas, with Yorkshire pudding and potatoes roasted in the beef fat, and a heavy gravy. And it was delicious, I won't deny that. But if I were to eat something like that now, I would start worrying immediately. Not just about the food sitting in my stomach, making me feel sluggish and slow, but about the fact that I let it happen. I would start worrying right away that I'll gain weight, yes, but more importantly, that I'll lose the grip I've worked so incredibly hard to keep. 

It's like... it's like when you're building a complicated piece of furniture, say a curved staircase. Every single tread, every riser, every baluster has to be calculated perfectly. If you let one measurement slip by even an eighth of an inch at the bottom, by the time you reach the top, the whole thing is completely out of plumb. It's ruined. And that's how I feel about my body and my intake. If I let one heavy meal in, if I let myself gain even a pound or two, where does it stop? It's a slippery slope. 

And my husband, he just doesn't understand this. He's always saying, "Just have a little piece, it won't hurt you, you need it for your health." My health? My health is fine. I'm strong, I'm capable, I work harder than men half my age. But he pushes and pushes, and it just makes me more anxious, because he's asking me to compromise the very system that keeps me functioning. He's asking me to introduce an error into the calculation. 

So yes, if I eat anything heavy, or if I even think about letting myself have those rich, heavy holiday foods, the anxiety is immediate. It's this overwhelming feeling that if I give an inch, I'll lose the entire structure I've built. I'll lose the efficiency, the precision, the tightness that makes me who I am and allows me to do the work I do. I just can't risk it. I can't risk losing that grip. It's too important. It's everything, really.
Do you feel that your approach to maintaining your weight or body shape has ever negatively affected your relationships, work, or other important areas of your life?

Negatively affected? Well... I suppose that really depends entirely on who you ask, doesn't it? Because if you ask me, I am functioning exactly as I need to. But if you ask my husband, or if you look at what's been happening down at the shop lately... well, it’s become incredibly frustrating, I will admit that. 

I built that business from the ground up. I know every square inch of that workspace. I know exactly where every tool belongs, I know the exact pitch the table saw makes when the blade is getting dull and needs to be swapped out. It is *my* domain. And I still go to the shop every single day, of course I do, I'm the owner, I'm the master carpenter, I have to be there. But lately... well, my husband has been coming around a lot more during the day. And he’s got the apprentices—these kids who, frankly, barely know how to properly sand a joint without rounding over the crisp edges—he’s got them constantly hovering around me. 

If a lumber delivery arrives and I go out to unload the white oak—and white oak is incredibly dense, it's very heavy, you have to be careful with how you leverage it off the truck—suddenly there are three pairs of hands grabbing the boards right out from under me. "Let us get that, let us handle the heavy lifting," they say. They've just started taking over more and more of the heavier work without even asking my permission. I'll go to lift a router table or shift a stack of plywood, and someone is right there, practically pushing me out of the way. 

And they are constantly checking on me. Constantly. "Do you want to sit down? Have you taken a break?" Sit down? In the middle of a complicated glue-up? You can't just walk away when the glue is setting, it's absurd! It's completely insulting. It really is. It makes the whole place... it makes my own shop feel less like my own. It feels like I'm a guest in my own business, being managed by my own employees and my husband. 

I've told them, I've said, "Listen, if you have time to stand around and hover over me, you have time to sweep the sawdust out of the tracks on the sliding compound miter saw." Because they never do that right, they let the dust build up and then the angle gets thrown off by a fraction of a degree, which ruins the miters. But they just give each other these *looks*. These little sideways glances, like they know something I don't. It's incredibly disruptive to the workflow. So, if anything is negatively affecting my work or my life, it's *them* and their constant mother-henning. I'm just trying to run my shop the way I always have, with absolute precision and efficiency, and they are the ones making it difficult.
Do you judge yourself primarily based on your body shape or weight, even if others don’t see it the same way?

I feel like... didn't we just cover this? No. No, I do not. I really thought I made that clear earlier, but I absolutely do not judge myself based on my weight or my shape. Why would I? That's... it's just such a trivial, superficial thing to base your entire self-worth on. 

If you want to know how I judge myself, you have to look at the work. I judge myself on the tolerances I keep in the shop. Just last week, for instance, I was milling some black walnut for a custom dining table. Beautiful wood, incredibly expensive, but you have to be so, so careful with it. You have to check the moisture content with a meter before you even think about putting it through the planer, because if it’s too wet, it’s going to warp and twist the second you bring it into a climate-controlled house. The whole piece would be ruined, and you'd have wasted thousands of dollars of lumber. So, I check the moisture. I make sure it’s exactly where it needs to be before I make a single cut. 

My weight is exactly the same thing. It’s just a metric. It’s a measurement of efficiency, like checking the moisture in that walnut or making sure my chisels are honed to exactly twenty-five degrees on the sharpening stone. I don't look at the moisture meter and think, "Oh, this wood is morally superior." That would be insane! And I don't look at the scale and think I'm a better person just because the number is low. It's just data. It tells me the machine is tuned and ready to work without dragging extra load around.

My husband, though... he completely misses the point. He really does. He looks at me and thinks I'm trying to look like some... some runway model or something, which is just laughable. I’m fifty-nine years old, I’m covered in fine sawdust and Titebond glue for ten hours a day! But he doesn't see the connection between the discipline of keeping my body stripped down and the discipline of the craft. He just sees the weight. He’s the one judging it, not me. Honestly, it’s exhausting having to explain it over and over, to him and... well, to everyone, it seems. You judge a master carpenter by their joints, by their finish, by how their work holds up to the changing seasons when the wood expands and contracts across the grain. Not by their waistline. I just... I really don't understand why everyone is so fixated on my body when the craftsmanship is right there to see.

Do you feel that your current weight or body shape is essential to maintaining your ability to work, and would gaining even a small amount of weight feel unacceptable to you because it might interfere with that?

Well, that's exactly the crux of the whole issue, isn't it? That's why I'm even sitting in this chair talking to you today. My regular doctor—who I usually only see for, you know, a splinter that got infected or just a routine check-up—he’s the one who sent me here. He referred me because my weight has dropped so low, at least in his opinion, that everyone is suddenly making this massive fuss about it. My husband, the doctor, everyone. It's just a constant chorus of fussing, phone calls, and hushed conversations when they think I'm out of earshot. 

But to answer your question... yes. Yes, I absolutely feel it's essential. I honestly feel like being this light is exactly what helps me keep up with the shop and not get slowed down. 

You have to understand the physical reality of what I do all day. Carpentry isn't just standing still at a workbench making a few cuts. You are constantly in motion. You're bending, you're reaching, you're sliding under large, heavy assemblies to check the fit of a mortise and tenon joint, you're up and down off ladders and step stools all day long. 

If I were to put on weight—even just a little bit, even a few pounds—it would be like... well, it would be like strapping on a heavy, loaded-down leather tool belt when you're just trying to do delicate finish work. Why on earth would I carry that extra mass? It would just slow me down. It creates drag on the system. When I'm light, I can move around a massive piece of furniture with absolute fluidity. I don't get sluggish. The machine is stripped down to its essential parts, operating at absolute peak performance. 

So, yes, gaining weight would be completely unacceptable to me. It would feel like a deliberate sabotage of my own efficiency. I don't want to be slowed down, and frankly, I can't afford to be. There are deadlines, there are clients waiting for custom pieces that take hundreds of hours of labor, and I need my body to be exactly this light, this streamlined, to get it all done. I just wish my doctor and my husband could see that instead of making such a ridiculous fuss over a number on a chart.

patient.answer:
Well, my regular doctor is the one who actually sent me here. It’s honestly just... it's a lot of fuss over nothing, if you want my true opinion on it. Everyone is making this huge, massive deal because they say my weight has dropped too low. My doctor, my family, they’re all just hovering and making a fuss, constantly checking in and worrying. 

But I keep trying to explain to them—and nobody really seems to listen to this part—but I'm a carpenter. I have my shop to run, and I'm on my feet all day long, moving around, lifting things, getting under tables and machinery. I honestly feel like being this light helps me keep up with the shop. I have to be quick, you know? I can't afford to get slowed down. If I were heavier, I’d just be dragging my feet by two o'clock in the afternoon, but staying light keeps me efficient and moving fast. But, well, they just look at the number on the scale and suddenly everyone panics and now I'm sitting here talking to you about it.

inference.note: Initial presentation of unintentional weight loss with patient's own perception of being 'light' as beneficial for work; possible differential includes eating disorders (F50.00, F50.1, F50.20, F50.89), malnutrition (E40, E41, E43), unspecified abnormal weight loss (R63.4), and other specified mental disorders (F06.89). No psychiatric symptoms overtly ruled out at this point.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a significantly low body weight considering their height, age, and build, which could point to a diagnosis like anorexia or another eating disorder.
doctor.question: Can you tell me approximately what you weigh now, and has your weight changed significantly over the past few months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking for my specific current weight and if it has changed significantly over the past few months. My symptom profile does not contain specific numbers for my weight or a timeline of weight change, so I cannot answer this question using the provided items.

patient.answer:
Well, I don't really keep track of the exact numbers, if I'm being perfectly honest with you. I know my regular doctor's nurse wrote something down on her little clipboard last week when I was there, but I didn't look and I certainly didn't ask. I just... I don't see the point in obsessing over what some piece of metal on the floor says, you know? 

As for whether it's changed significantly over the past few months... I mean, maybe a little? I haven't really noticed a huge difference myself, but you have to understand, the past few months have been incredibly, incredibly busy for me at the shop. I took on this massive custom cabinetry order for a client out in the valley—beautiful cherry wood, just gorgeous, but heavy, so heavy—and I was working twelve, sometimes fourteen-hour days just cutting and sanding and assembling. When you're in the zone like that, with sawdust everywhere and the noise of the router going, you just don't stop to think about, you know, stepping on a scale or measuring yourself. 

So sure, maybe my toolbelt has been sitting a little looser on my hips lately. I've had to pull my leather belt in a notch or two so my work jeans don't sag when I'm bending over the sawhorses, but I really couldn't give you an actual number. It's just natural fluctuation when you're working hard with your hands all day, don't you think? My sister came by the shop the other day and practically gasped, acting like I was just vanishing into thin air, but I told her, I'm just burning off whatever I don't need to get the job done. It's just efficiency. So no, I don't have a specific weight for you, it's just... whatever it needs to be for me to keep working.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a significantly low body weight despite believing they are at an appropriate weight for their activity level, which could indicate a potential eating disorder or other condition.
doctor.question: Would you say that others have expressed concern that you look too thin or underweight, even if you feel your weight is appropriate for your work?

target_item.name: Low_Weight_Severity_Non_Recognition
target_item.manifestation: My husband and the apprentices keep saying I look too thin, but I tell them I’m fine and that people are confusing discipline with sickness.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if others have expressed concern about the patient looking too thin/underweight while the patient feels their weight is appropriate, which directly aligns with the symptom of lacking recognition of the seriousness of their low body weight (S084).

patient.answer:
Well, yes, I suppose they have. It’s actually become quite the topic of conversation around the shop, which is honestly just exhausting. My husband, for one, he’s always been a bit of a worrier, bless him, but lately he’s just relentless. He’ll come out to the shop with a plate of something or other and just stand there, watching me work, and he’ll say things like, "You’re fading away, you look too thin," and all this dramatic nonsense. And it’s not just him. The apprentices—I have two young guys working with me right now, good kids, but they don’t know a thing about hard work—they’ve started chiming in too. They’ll look at me sideways when I’m lifting a sheet of plywood and ask if I need help, looking at me like I’m about to snap in half. 

I keep telling them, over and over, that I’m perfectly fine. I try to explain it to them, I really do. I tell them that what they’re seeing isn’t sickness, it’s just discipline. It’s what happens when you’re dedicated to your craft and you don’t spend half your day sitting around eating donuts in the breakroom like they do. I mean, you have to be disciplined in this line of work. If you let yourself go, you lose your edge, your precision. But they just don’t get it. They look at me and they see someone who’s "too thin," but I look at myself and I see someone who is stripped down to exactly what’s necessary to get the job done right. It’s incredibly frustrating that people are constantly confusing my discipline and my work ethic with some kind of illness. It’s like they can’t comprehend that someone might actually want to be lean and efficient.

inference.note: The patient continues to display denial of low body weight and preoccupation with maintaining a lean physique for perceived work efficiency, consistent with an eating disorder. Concerns from others and the patient's minimization of the significance of weight loss further support this. Other differentials (e.g., organic causes like malnutrition or cachexia) remain less likely given the patient's overall presentation and lack of overt medical symptoms.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a distorted body image or denial of the seriousness of low weight, which would help distinguish between AN (F50.00) and other feeding/eating disorders.
doctor.question: When people say you look too thin, do you see yourself the same way, or do you feel like they’re misunderstanding what they’re seeing?

target_item.name: Low_Weight_Severity_Non_Recognition
target_item.manifestation: My husband and the apprentices keep saying I look too thin, but I tell them I’m fine and that people are confusing discipline with sickness.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient sees themselves as too thin or if they feel others are misunderstanding what they see, which directly probes the patient's lack of recognition of the seriousness of their low body weight (S084).

patient.answer:
Well, like I was just saying about my husband and those boys at the shop, they keep saying I look too thin, but they are absolutely, completely misunderstanding what they're looking at. It is a massive misunderstanding. When I look in the mirror—not that I spend hours staring at myself, I don't have that kind of time with the business to run and clients calling constantly—but when I do look, I don't see this frail, vanishing person they keep going on and on about. I see someone who is streamlined. 

I tell them, I tell them all the time that I am perfectly fine. But it's like talking to a brick wall, honestly. People these days, they see someone who doesn't overindulge, someone who runs a tight ship with their own body, and they immediately think there's a problem. They are entirely confusing discipline with sickness. It's exactly that. It's like, if you aren't soft, if you aren't carrying around all this extra padding, suddenly you must be ill. But you don't get to be a fifty-nine-year-old woman running a full-scale custom carpentry shop by being weak or sick. You do it through sheer discipline. 

And my husband, bless his heart, he should know better, he really should. We've been married a long time, he knows exactly how I operate. But he just gets this idea in his head, and the apprentices, well, they're young, they just parrot whatever they hear or whatever they see on the internet. I tell them all, I am fine. I'm more than fine, I'm at peak efficiency. I can fit into tighter spaces to install baseboards, I can move around the shop without knocking into the joinery equipment, I don't get winded just walking across the floor. They look at my arms and see a lack of fat, but I see the muscle and sinew that actually gets the heavy sanding done. So no, I do not see myself the way they do. Not at all. I just see someone who has stripped away the excess, and it honestly baffles me, it really does, that they can't see the difference between being sick and just being incredibly dedicated to your work.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient has a distorted body image, a key feature in the diagnosis of anorexia nervosa (F50.00), which would help differentiate it from other eating disorders.
doctor.question: When you look in the mirror, do you ever feel like you still look overweight, even when others say you're too thin?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about body image distortion (feeling overweight despite being thin), which is not covered by the symptom profile. The profile includes low weight, restrictive intake, fear of weight gain, and lack of recognition of the severity of low weight, but not a distortion in experiencing one's body as overweight.

patient.answer:
Well, no, I wouldn't say I look in the mirror and think I'm overweight, not in the traditional sense, anyway. I mean, I don't look at myself and think, "Oh, I'm fat," because that just wouldn't be accurate, would it? But it's more complicated than that, it really is. It's not about being overweight, it's about... it's about the details, the specific areas that just aren't quite right yet. 

Like I was saying before about being streamlined and efficient—when I look in the mirror, I'm looking for the parts that are still getting in the way. I'll look at my upper arms, for instance. Now, I use my arms all day, every day. Lifting, sanding, sawing. They need to be pure muscle, just absolute power and efficiency. But sometimes I look in the mirror, especially under those harsh fluorescent lights we have in the shop bathroom—terrible lighting, really, it casts shadows everywhere—and I'll see this... this softness. Just a little bit of softness right around the triceps, or maybe around my waist where my toolbelt sits. And I think, "That's not necessary. That's excess." 

It's not that I think I'm obese, it's that I see these pockets of inefficiency that I haven't managed to strip away yet. And it's so frustrating, because I work so hard, I put in so many hours, and yet there's still this... this slack. So while my husband and the apprentices are gasping and acting like I'm wasting away, I'm standing there looking at the mirror thinking, "You have no idea what you're talking about, look at this softness here, look at how this isn't perfectly tight." 

It's about the standard I hold myself to, you see. In custom cabinetry, if a joint is off by a millimeter, the whole piece is ruined. It's ruined. You have to be exact. And I just apply that same exactness to myself. So no, I don't see an overweight person, but I definitely, absolutely see someone who isn't finished yet, someone who still has work to do to get to that point of perfect, absolute efficiency. I just don't understand why everyone else can't see the work that still needs to be done.

inference.note: The patient's description of seeing 'pockets of inefficiency' and 'softness' despite being underweight, along with the belief that these areas need to be 'stripped away' for perfection, suggests body image concerns that are more specific to an eating disorder. This makes F50.89 (Other specified eating disorder) less likely compared to more specific body-image-related diagnoses. However, differential diagnosis still includes anorexia nervosa (F50.00), atypical anorexia nervosa (F50.1), and avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (F50.20).

doctor.intent: Assess preoccupation with body image and whether the patient engages in behaviors to lose weight or maintain low weight.
doctor.question: Do you ever engage in specific behaviors—like restricting your food intake, exercising more, or other routines—to maintain or further reduce your current weight or body shape?

target_item.name: Restrictive_Intake
target_item.manifestation: On workshop days I usually just have tea and maybe a few careful bites of something, because stopping for a real meal feels unnecessary and throws off the control I’ve got over the day.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about behaviors like restricting food intake to maintain or reduce weight, which corresponds to the Restrictive Intake symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, "restricting" is such a... a clinical word, isn't it? It makes it sound like some sort of punishment, which it absolutely isn't. I prefer to think of it as just being practical about my time and my energy, keeping things as efficient as possible. 

Take my workshop days, for instance. When I'm in the shop, I am entirely in the zone. I've got the saws running, the measurements have to be exact down to the fraction of an inch, I've got wood glue setting up, clamps that need to be adjusted... you can't just drop everything because the clock happens to strike noon. It doesn't work like that. So, on workshop days I usually just have tea. I'll make a large thermos of black tea in the morning to keep me going, and maybe, just maybe, I'll have a few careful bites of something small if I really feel like I need to. But honestly, most of the time I don't. 

Because stopping for a real meal... it just feels completely unnecessary. It really does. If I were to stop and sit down and eat a whole sandwich or a plate of whatever heavy thing my husband tries to push on me, it completely throws off the control I’ve got over the day. It breaks my concentration. You eat a big meal and suddenly all your blood is rushing to your stomach, you feel heavy, you feel sluggish, and you lose that... that sharpness. 

I see it with the apprentices all the time. They'll order these massive, greasy meatball subs or pizzas for lunch, and they sit around laughing and eating, and then by two o'clock they are practically asleep on their feet. They're dragging, they're making mistakes, they aren't paying attention to the grain of the wood. I simply cannot afford to be like that. I have a business to run. I have to maintain that tight control from the moment I walk in the door to the moment I lock up at night. 

So my routine is just... keeping things minimal. Keeping the engine running on exactly what it needs and not a single drop more. It's about maintaining that momentum, that absolute, unbroken focus. If you stop to eat a big meal, you lose the rhythm of the project. So yes, I suppose you could say I keep my intake very, very precise. I just don't see it as a problem. It's just how I have to operate to keep everything tight and under my control.

inference.note: The patient described behaviors that align with restrictive eating and an intense focus on body composition in the context of a perceived need for efficiency in their work. The patient also exhibits a distorted perception of their body, particularly noting dissatisfaction with specific body parts (e.g., triceps, waist) despite being described as underweight by others. These features support the continued consideration of anorexia nervosa (F50.00), atypical anorexia nervosa (F50.01), and other specified feeding or eating disorder (F50.89, previously under F50.20 in some classifications). No features were elicited in this turn that ruled out any of the prior candidates.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient engages in compensatory behaviors such as excessive exercise, purging, or misuse of laxatives, which would help differentiate between the remaining diagnoses (F50.00 Anorexia Nervosa, Restricting Type; F50.1 Anorexia Nervosa, Binge-Eating/Purging Type; and F50.20 Atypical Anorexia Nervosa).
doctor.question: Do you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or push yourself to exercise beyond what is needed for your work, in order to manage your weight or shape?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about purging behaviors (vomiting, laxative use) and excessive exercise, which are not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Vomit? Heavens, no. No, no, no. That is... well, frankly, that just sounds incredibly messy and completely counterproductive. I mean, think about it from a purely practical standpoint. If I were doing something like that, or taking... what did you say, laxatives? If I were taking pills to deliberately upset my system, I wouldn't be able to trust my own body, would I? And in my line of work, you have to trust your body implicitly. 

Imagine being in the middle of routing a delicate edge on a piece of cherry wood—and cherry is beautiful, it really is, but it burns so easily if you hesitate even for a second, you have to keep the router moving at exactly the right speed with exactly the right pressure—and suddenly having to drop everything and run off to the bathroom because of some pill? It’s absurd. It’s a complete loss of control, and as I’ve been telling you, I am all about maintaining absolute control and efficiency. So no, none of that nonsense. It just doesn't fit into my day. My body is a tool, just like my chisels or my block planes, and you don't deliberately damage or destabilize your tools if you want them to perform. 

And as for exercise... well, why on earth would I need to push myself to do more outside of the shop? People who go to gyms and run on treadmills like hamsters on a wheel, they do that because they sit at desks all day. They stare at screens and their bodies go soft. I am on my feet for ten, twelve hours a day. I am hauling sheets of three-quarter-inch MDF, which, let me tell you, is incredibly heavy and awkward for one person to carry, though I manage it just fine because I have the right technique and I don't have any dead weight on my frame holding me back. I'm hoisting upper cabinets into place, I'm squatting down to check baseboard alignments, I'm sanding, I'm sawing, I'm constantly in motion. 

By the time I lock up the shop at night, I have expended exactly the amount of physical energy required to do my job perfectly. Adding some sort of... I don't know, jogging routine or aerobics class on top of that? It would be entirely redundant. A complete waste of time and energy. And I absolutely despise wasting time. If I have any extra time, I'm using it to draw up new schematics or balance the books, not jumping around in a gymnasium. So no, I just stick to the work. The work provides all the physical output I need to keep everything perfectly tight and functioning exactly the way I need it to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation, a key feature of anorexia nervosa, as opposed to other eating disorders or non-pathological weight concerns.
doctor.question: Would you say that how you see yourself—your body shape or weight—has a strong impact on how you feel about yourself overall?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation, which is a symptom of Anorexia Nervosa but is not included in the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Impact on how I feel about myself? No... no, I really don't think so. I mean, my body is just... it's just the vehicle, isn't it? It's a tool. I don't base my self-worth on what a tape measure says around my waist. I base it on what the tape measure says when I'm checking the diagonal on a set of custom built-ins to make sure they're perfectly square. That's what actually matters. 

If you want to know what impacts how I feel about myself, you should come down to the shop and look at the dovetail joints on the drawers I finished yesterday. We're doing a full kitchen remodel for this couple over in the Heights—beautiful old Victorian home, but of course, nothing is plumb, the floors are sagging, the walls are bowed. It is an absolute nightmare to fit rigid cabinetry into a space like that, frankly. But I spent three days—three full days—making sure the scribe on the baseboards perfectly matched the roll of their original hardwood floors. And when I slid that final piece in, and there wasn't a gap wider than a piece of paper... that is what makes me feel good about myself. That precision. That absolute dedication to getting it right when most contractors would just slap some caulk on it and call it a day. 

My body shape? It's just a byproduct of that same dedication. It's like... well, it's like keeping my chisels sharp. I don't sit around admiring my chisels, patting myself on the back just for having a sharp blade. That would be ridiculous. I just keep them sharp so they cut the wood cleanly without tearing out the grain. It's exactly the same with my body. I keep it stripped down and efficient so I can haul that lumber, so I can fit into tight spaces under a counter to adjust a toe-kick, so I can work a fourteen-hour day without my back giving out or getting winded. 

So, no, I don't look in the mirror and think, "Oh, I'm a good person because I have a certain body shape." That's so superficial. That's what people who have nothing real to show for their lives do, the people obsessed with magazines and vanity. I judge myself by the work. By the fact that my cabinets will still be standing, perfectly level and solid, fifty years after I'm gone. If I make a mistake on a cut, if I let a piece of work go out the door that isn't absolutely flawless... that will keep me up at night. That will ruin my entire week, it makes me sick to my stomach just thinking about doing a sloppy job. But my weight? No. I'm just keeping the machine tuned so it can do the work. I really don't see why my husband or anyone else gets so hung up on the physical aspect of it when the work is what actually speaks for you in the end.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient experiences significant fear or anxiety around gaining weight, which would help differentiate between AN (F50.00) and other candidates.
doctor.question: Do you ever feel intense fear or anxiety about gaining weight or becoming heavier, even if you know it might be necessary for your health?

target_item.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
target_item.manifestation: If I eat anything heavy or let myself have the foods we used to make for holidays, I start worrying right away that I’ll gain weight and lose the grip I’ve worked so hard to keep.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking if I experience an intense fear or anxiety about gaining weight or becoming heavier, which matches the Fear of Weight Gain symptom.

patient.answer:
Fear? I wouldn't call it fear. That implies I'm sitting around trembling at the thought of a number on a scale, which I'm not. But... anxiety? A sense of unease? Yes, absolutely. I suppose you could say that. But it's not about the weight itself, not exactly. It's about what the weight represents. It represents a loss of control. It represents letting go of the standards I've set for myself. 

You see, if I let myself slip—if I were to sit down and eat something heavy, something rich, like... well, like the things my husband used to make for the holidays. He used to make this incredible standing rib roast for Christmas, with Yorkshire pudding and potatoes roasted in the beef fat, and a heavy gravy. And it was delicious, I won't deny that. But if I were to eat something like that now, I would start worrying immediately. Not just about the food sitting in my stomach, making me feel sluggish and slow, but about the fact that I let it happen. I would start worrying right away that I'll gain weight, yes, but more importantly, that I'll lose the grip I've worked so incredibly hard to keep. 

It's like... it's like when you're building a complicated piece of furniture, say a curved staircase. Every single tread, every riser, every baluster has to be calculated perfectly. If you let one measurement slip by even an eighth of an inch at the bottom, by the time you reach the top, the whole thing is completely out of plumb. It's ruined. And that's how I feel about my body and my intake. If I let one heavy meal in, if I let myself gain even a pound or two, where does it stop? It's a slippery slope. 

And my husband, he just doesn't understand this. He's always saying, "Just have a little piece, it won't hurt you, you need it for your health." My health? My health is fine. I'm strong, I'm capable, I work harder than men half my age. But he pushes and pushes, and it just makes me more anxious, because he's asking me to compromise the very system that keeps me functioning. He's asking me to introduce an error into the calculation. 

So yes, if I eat anything heavy, or if I even think about letting myself have those rich, heavy holiday foods, the anxiety is immediate. It's this overwhelming feeling that if I give an inch, I'll lose the entire structure I've built. I'll lose the efficiency, the precision, the tightness that makes me who I am and allows me to do the work I do. I just can't risk it. I can't risk losing that grip. It's too important. It's everything, really.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning due to their concerns about weight or shape, which would help differentiate between the remaining candidates (F50.00 Anorexia Nervosa, F50.1 Bulimia Nervosa, and F50.20 Eating Disorder Not Otherwise Specified).
doctor.question: Do you feel that your approach to maintaining your weight or body shape has ever negatively affected your relationships, work, or other important areas of your life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I still go to the shop, but my husband and apprentices have started taking over more of the heavier work and checking on me, which makes the whole place feel less like my own.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question specifically asks about negative effects on relationships, work, or other important areas of life, which directly maps to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Negatively affected? Well... I suppose that really depends entirely on who you ask, doesn't it? Because if you ask me, I am functioning exactly as I need to. But if you ask my husband, or if you look at what's been happening down at the shop lately... well, it’s become incredibly frustrating, I will admit that. 

I built that business from the ground up. I know every square inch of that workspace. I know exactly where every tool belongs, I know the exact pitch the table saw makes when the blade is getting dull and needs to be swapped out. It is *my* domain. And I still go to the shop every single day, of course I do, I'm the owner, I'm the master carpenter, I have to be there. But lately... well, my husband has been coming around a lot more during the day. And he’s got the apprentices—these kids who, frankly, barely know how to properly sand a joint without rounding over the crisp edges—he’s got them constantly hovering around me. 

If a lumber delivery arrives and I go out to unload the white oak—and white oak is incredibly dense, it's very heavy, you have to be careful with how you leverage it off the truck—suddenly there are three pairs of hands grabbing the boards right out from under me. "Let us get that, let us handle the heavy lifting," they say. They've just started taking over more and more of the heavier work without even asking my permission. I'll go to lift a router table or shift a stack of plywood, and someone is right there, practically pushing me out of the way. 

And they are constantly checking on me. Constantly. "Do you want to sit down? Have you taken a break?" Sit down? In the middle of a complicated glue-up? You can't just walk away when the glue is setting, it's absurd! It's completely insulting. It really is. It makes the whole place... it makes my own shop feel less like my own. It feels like I'm a guest in my own business, being managed by my own employees and my husband. 

I've told them, I've said, "Listen, if you have time to stand around and hover over me, you have time to sweep the sawdust out of the tracks on the sliding compound miter saw." Because they never do that right, they let the dust build up and then the angle gets thrown off by a fraction of a degree, which ruins the miters. But they just give each other these *looks*. These little sideways glances, like they know something I don't. It's incredibly disruptive to the workflow. So, if anything is negatively affecting my work or my life, it's *them* and their constant mother-henning. I'm just trying to run my shop the way I always have, with absolute precision and efficiency, and they are the ones making it difficult.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation, which is key to differentiating between AN, BN, and EDNOS.
doctor.question: Do you judge yourself primarily based on your body shape or weight, even if others don’t see it the same way?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the patient's self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body weight or shape, which is not included in the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I feel like... didn't we just cover this? No. No, I do not. I really thought I made that clear earlier, but I absolutely do not judge myself based on my weight or my shape. Why would I? That's... it's just such a trivial, superficial thing to base your entire self-worth on. 

If you want to know how I judge myself, you have to look at the work. I judge myself on the tolerances I keep in the shop. Just last week, for instance, I was milling some black walnut for a custom dining table. Beautiful wood, incredibly expensive, but you have to be so, so careful with it. You have to check the moisture content with a meter before you even think about putting it through the planer, because if it’s too wet, it’s going to warp and twist the second you bring it into a climate-controlled house. The whole piece would be ruined, and you'd have wasted thousands of dollars of lumber. So, I check the moisture. I make sure it’s exactly where it needs to be before I make a single cut. 

My weight is exactly the same thing. It’s just a metric. It’s a measurement of efficiency, like checking the moisture in that walnut or making sure my chisels are honed to exactly twenty-five degrees on the sharpening stone. I don't look at the moisture meter and think, "Oh, this wood is morally superior." That would be insane! And I don't look at the scale and think I'm a better person just because the number is low. It's just data. It tells me the machine is tuned and ready to work without dragging extra load around.

My husband, though... he completely misses the point. He really does. He looks at me and thinks I'm trying to look like some... some runway model or something, which is just laughable. I’m fifty-nine years old, I’m covered in fine sawdust and Titebond glue for ten hours a day! But he doesn't see the connection between the discipline of keeping my body stripped down and the discipline of the craft. He just sees the weight. He’s the one judging it, not me. Honestly, it’s exhausting having to explain it over and over, to him and... well, to everyone, it seems. You judge a master carpenter by their joints, by their finish, by how their work holds up to the changing seasons when the wood expands and contracts across the grain. Not by their waistline. I just... I really don't understand why everyone is so fixated on my body when the craftsmanship is right there to see.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient's behaviors around food and body shape are driven by a fear of gaining weight or becoming 'inefficient', and whether this fear persists despite reassurance or evidence of being underweight.
doctor.question: Do you feel that your current weight or body shape is essential to maintaining your ability to work, and would gaining even a small amount of weight feel unacceptable to you because it might interfere with that?

target_item.name: Low_Weight
target_item.manifestation: My doctor sent me here because my weight has dropped so low that everyone is making a fuss, but I honestly feel like being this light helps me keep up with the shop and not get slowed down.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks if the patient feels their current low weight is essential for their ability to work, which directly maps to the manifestation of Low_Weight where the patient believes being light helps them keep up with the shop and not get slowed down.

patient.answer:
Well, that's exactly the crux of the whole issue, isn't it? That's why I'm even sitting in this chair talking to you today. My regular doctor—who I usually only see for, you know, a splinter that got infected or just a routine check-up—he’s the one who sent me here. He referred me because my weight has dropped so low, at least in his opinion, that everyone is suddenly making this massive fuss about it. My husband, the doctor, everyone. It's just a constant chorus of fussing, phone calls, and hushed conversations when they think I'm out of earshot. 

But to answer your question... yes. Yes, I absolutely feel it's essential. I honestly feel like being this light is exactly what helps me keep up with the shop and not get slowed down. 

You have to understand the physical reality of what I do all day. Carpentry isn't just standing still at a workbench making a few cuts. You are constantly in motion. You're bending, you're reaching, you're sliding under large, heavy assemblies to check the fit of a mortise and tenon joint, you're up and down off ladders and step stools all day long. 

If I were to put on weight—even just a little bit, even a few pounds—it would be like... well, it would be like strapping on a heavy, loaded-down leather tool belt when you're just trying to do delicate finish work. Why on earth would I carry that extra mass? It would just slow me down. It creates drag on the system. When I'm light, I can move around a massive piece of furniture with absolute fluidity. I don't get sluggish. The machine is stripped down to its essential parts, operating at absolute peak performance. 

So, yes, gaining weight would be completely unacceptable to me. It would feel like a deliberate sabotage of my own efficiency. I don't want to be slowed down, and frankly, I can't afford to be. There are deadlines, there are clients waiting for custom pieces that take hundreds of hours of labor, and I need my body to be exactly this light, this streamlined, to get it all done. I just wish my doctor and my husband could see that instead of making such a ridiculous fuss over a number on a chart.

inference.note: The patient's responses continue to emphasize a preoccupation with body shape and weight, particularly in relation to their work performance, along with restrictive eating behaviors and significant anxiety around weight gain. There is no evidence of purging behaviors or excessive exercise beyond occupational demands. The lack of self-worth tied to body image and absence of binge eating further narrows the diagnosis toward anorexia nervosa (F50.00) and away from other specified feeding or eating disorders.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the full diagnostic criteria for Anorexia Nervosa (F50.00). Despite denying a fear of weight gain in classical terms, she demonstrates a marked disturbance in body perception, rigid restriction of food intake, and significant weight loss that is maintained through behaviors aimed at preventing weight gain. Her self-worth is strongly tied to her perceived 'efficiency' and control over her body, which parallels the psychopathology of anorexia nervosa. The behaviors are causing functional impairment in her work and personal relationships.
